claims.text: Q235 steel in its untreated pre-exposure state has a naturally formed native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer protects Q235 steel from corrosion at room temperature.
The native oxide becomes unstable at 700–900 °C in the presence of aggressive salt.
High-temperature instability of the oxide scale accelerates corrosion of the underlying Q235 steel.
Oxide-layer integrity and composition govern whether Q235 retains corrosion protection.
At room temperature, the oxide acts as a robust corrosion barrier.
At high temperature, aggressive salt induces oxide fluxing or phase changes.
Salt-induced oxide alteration causes pore formation or spallation.
Pore formation or spallation exposes the underlying steel and thereby accelerates corrosion.
Room-temperature salt-exposed Q235 will exhibit minimal mass change.
Room-temperature salt-exposed Q235 will retain an intact protective oxide film.
Q235 exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C will undergo significantly greater mass loss than the room-temperature salt-exposed reference.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce oxide defects and increased surface roughness relative to the room-temperature reference.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply specifically to Q235 steel with its native pre-exposure surface.
Substantial alloying or an engineered coating or HEA cladding may change oxide behavior and corrosion response.
The exact oxide compositional and phase transitions during high-temperature salt exposure are not established.
